_note:
A gate's time budget is a DECLARED MULTIPLE of a MEASURED runtime, never a round number (#94, ruling n=744): budget_sec = margin_x x measured_sec. A cap picked by feel is uncalibrated in both directions -- too low, it kills a healthy gate and reports a timeout as a verdict; too high, it hides a hung one. The budget VALUES are the process owner's, never the implementing lane's (n=574 PART 5).

THE MARGIN, AND ITS BASIS. margin_x is a stated function of the measurement, not a number picked by feel, because the measured spread is not uniform across the range. A 13-run probe of three gates spanning the range (tests/test_single_writer.py, tests/test_patrol_host_state.py, tests/test_ledger_no_shrink.py; 2026-09-20) measured a worst within-run spread of 2.48x, and the audit-vs-standalone factor on the slowest gate was 1.83x. The relative spread SHRINKS as runtime grows (2.35x at 0.11 s against 1.15x at 16.11 s), because a short runtime is dominated by fixed process overhead whose variance is a large fraction of a small total. A flat relative margin would therefore give the LEAST headroom exactly where the noise is relatively largest. So margin_x = 4.0 + 0.75 / measured_sec: the asymptotic 4.0 is a stated safety factor above the worst measured cross-context factor (1.83x), and the 0.75-second term is the largest absolute jitter the probe measured among the short gates (tests/test_patrol_host_state.py, 0.48 s to 1.20 s, i.e. 0.72 s) rounded up to the next quarter second -- the fixed overhead that dominates a short runtime, expressed as a margin. The constant is 0.75 and not a rounder value for a reason worth stating: with 4.0 as the asymptotic factor the product is 4 x measured + K, so a fixed term whose fractional part complements that of 4 x measured lands the budget on an exact integer -- under a 0.72 s term two gates in this set did exactly that, one of them reproducing the very hardcoded cap this manifest replaces. A budget that reads as a picked number is the ambiguity the manifest exists to remove. budget_sec is the product rounded to 2 dp; margin_x is stored rounded to 3 dp and the product is taken from the unrounded value, so recomputing from measured_sec reproduces the declared budget to within 0.01 s.

THE CLOSED FORM, AND WHY IT IS NOT A DEFECT. Because margin_x is 4.0 + 0.75 / measured_sec, the budget expands to budget_sec = 4.0 x measured_sec + 0.75 -- a fixed 0.75-second term on top of a flat 4x factor. Measured over all 44 entries (2026-09-20): 36 declared bases sit at or above real wall time, the audit-vs-standalone delta is NOT constant (stdev 4.05 s pytest-form, 2.90 s script-form), and only four entries carry a positive delta above 1.0 s, three of which the margin absorbs. The fixed term is a design characteristic of the margin, not a defect in it, so no uniform correction is applied: one that was would be wrong in both directions (YAGNI).

measured_at is the ABSOLUTE revision the runtimes were measured at, never a relative revision. measured_sec is WHOLE-COMMAND WALL-CLOCK SECONDS for the gate at that revision: the elapsed time from process start to process exit, which INCLUDES interpreter startup, pytest's own import and its collection pass. That is exactly the number python3 tools/audit.py records as duration_sec, so no new instrument is needed; where several samples of one gate exist, the WORST OBSERVED one is the basis, because a budget must contain the slow tail and not the median.

THE BASIS IS RE-DERIVED ON A CONTAINMENT EVENT, NOT ON EVERY FRESH SAMPLE: when the registered command's RUNNER FORM changes, so the declared basis no longer describes what runs (#125 leg B), or when a measured sample EXHAUSTS the budget and the audit reports UNKNOWN. A fresh sample that stays inside the cap is absorbed by margin_x, whose stated job is exactly that variation; re-basing on every new maximum would ratchet the cap toward the too-high direction named above (#128, ruling n=823).

THE PREDICATE THIS IS NOT, AND WHY IT IS NAMED HERE. pytest's own summary line -- "12 passed in 0.26s" -- times only the collected test BODIES and EXCLUDES interpreter startup, import and collection. On tests/test_board_intake_recorded.py that line reads 0.14-0.37 s while the whole command runs 2.89-6.47 s standalone and 2.09 s through the audit: a 17x gap, and a budget of 2.07 s derived from the summary line killed a healthy gate. It is a UNIT/PREDICATE MISMATCH -- right digits, wrong clock -- the same class as a character cap standing in for a token cap, and it is invisible because both forms are seconds. So the field carries ONE predicate, stated above, and the summary line is not it. CAVEAT ON THIS MEASUREMENT: the run that produced these numbers was DEGRADED (one gate failing) and was taken with a peer lane's writes in flight, so the values are conservative upper bounds on a quiet-tree runtime. That makes the declared budgets generous, not tight.

THE DEFAULT (#208). A gate with no entry uses default.budget_sec, and the audit PRINTS which gates used it -- a declared default with a printed population is not an exempt-by-silence surface, an unprinted fallback would be. The default is margin_x x the LARGEST MEASURED RUNTIME AMONG THE UNDECLARED POPULATION -- the gates that actually fall through to it -- re-derived whenever that population changes, with the population and the measuring revision stated beside the value. It is NOT the largest DECLARED entry: that relation was asserted here until 2026-09-28 and NOTHING asserted it, so it went false silently the day an entry landed above the default (118.51 against 1008.75, 8.51x apart), and tests/test_questions.py -- which then carried no entry and ran 69.85 s unloaded -- was killed at the fallback on two independent runs, reporting UNKNOWN rather than a pass or a failure. It now carries its OWN entry (#230), which is why it left the population below: the gate that supplied the default's basis no longer falls through to the number that used to kill it. Bounding by the undeclared population is also what keeps one outlier entry from loosening 23 gates to accommodate it, which is the 'too high hides a hung gate' direction ruling n=823 refuses. tools/gate_budget.py REFUSES a stated derivation that cannot contain its own population, sits below its own basis, disagrees with its recorded largest, or omits a gate now falling through; a manifest stating NO derivation asserts nothing and keeps loading, which is the shape registry/gates.example.json ships on purpose. THE POPULATION'S OWN PROVENANCE, stated because a number without it is unreproducible. Each entry is whole-command wall-clock seconds under the predicate above. Entries whose gate blob matched a completed audit run carry that run's duration_sec, taken at load 1-4; entries whose blob had moved before their turn carried the MINIMUM of three standalone passes at load 16-24, so those few are conservative UPPER BOUNDS on a quiet-tree runtime -- the same caveat this file already carries for its declared entries. The single max deciding the value below is tests/test_synthesize_insights.py's 17.13 s, measured at load median 19.20 -- so the default now DOES rest on a loaded sample, which is #226's point: a quiet-window base does not bound the box's operative load. The previous max was tests/test_questions.py's 69.85 s, an UNLOADED measurement of the gate that has since been declared.

A budget exhausted is UNKNOWN: never green, never a plain failure, and its recorded duration is the MEASURED elapsed time, never a hardcoded zero. (the reader half of #94 landed at commit 48caa2c: tools/audit.py now returns exit_code 124 with duration_sec MEASURED on a budget exhaustion, flags the result UNKNOWN, and prints three states -- PASS, FAIL and UNKNOWN -- so an exhausted budget is never silently killed and never silently green.)

This file is this box's DECLARED manifest. The template ships the SHAPE only, as TEMPLATE/registry/gates.example.json, because a bootstrapped factory has no measurement of this box and must not inherit one: a gate that cannot pass where it is copied is not a gate, it is a tax on every new factory.

THE INVOCATION MODE (#195, ruled n=1340). `modes` declares, per gate, WHICH convention `tools/audit.py` invokes it by -- `script` (the file is run directly, so its `__main__` block owns the verdict) or `pytest` (it is collected, so the test functions own it). The split is INTENDED and is not converted (#144: a gate's form is a property of what it tests, not a uniform). What was missing was the DECLARATION: a member wiring the kit's gates into a pytest-based CI enforces only the pytest-invoked population, and a green CI then reads as 'the gates passed' when a script-invoked gate was never collected. The mode is declared at the CALL SITE's form, never the file's shape -- a file can be dual-shaped, so 'the file has def test_' does not answer 'what does the audit run it as'. tests/test_gate_invocation_mode.py asserts this map against the call sites themselves.
